title: Pushes and pulls: every force points somewhere

summary.text: This unit is about pushes and pulls. Scientists call every push and every pull a force. Forces can start things moving, stop them, speed them up, slow them down and turn them. Every force points in a direction, so we draw it as an arrow. A longer arrow means a bigger force. Forces always come in pairs: when you push a wall, the wall pushes you back. Some forces work by touching, and some, like magnets and gravity, pull from far away. Deep down, every push you feel is tiny electrons pushing each other apart. And scientists still argue about what a force really is.
summary.art: A child pushing a swing and pulling a kite string at once, with a bold arrow drawn on each, one pointing forward and one pointing up the string.

intro.hook: Try this. Stand facing a wall, about one step away. Put both palms on the wall and push. Did the wall move? Did you? Something pushed you back. What was it?
intro.text: In a tug of war, everyone watches the rope. Each team pulls as hard as it can. One team slides forward and loses. Most people say the winners pulled harder on the rope. But here is a puzzle. The rope is one rope. Can it pull one end harder than the other? This unit is about pushes and pulls, the forces that move everything. By the end, you will be able to answer the rope puzzle. You will also know where to look to win.
intro.art: A village tug of war on wet grass, a chalk line in the middle, one team leaning low with heels dug in, the other team standing tall.

outcomes: I can say that a force is a push or a pull, and sort everyday actions into pushes, pulls, or both.
I can say what forces do to moving things: start them, stop them, speed them up, slow them down and change their direction.
I can explain that every force acts in a direction, and that the same push in a different direction gives a different result.
I can draw a force as an arrow. It starts on the thing, points the way of the push or pull, and is longer for a bigger force. I can use arrows to say which way a tug of war will move.
I can explain that forces come in pairs. When I push or pull something, it pushes or pulls me back.
I can tell touching forces from forces that work from far away, like magnets and gravity.
I can explain some deep ideas. Touching pushes are electrons pushing apart. Muscles can only pull. The Earth and I pull on each other. Scientists still argue about what a force really is.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces can start or stop things, speed them up, slow them down, turn them or change their shape.
terms.example: Kicking a football is a force. So is pulling open a drawer.
terms.art: A foot kicking a ball and a hand pulling a drawer, each with a bold arrow.

terms.meaning: A force that moves something away from you, or presses on it.
terms.example: You push a door shut. You push the button on a mixer.
terms.art: A hand pushing a door shut, the arrow pointing away from the hand.

terms.meaning: A force that moves something towards you, or drags it along behind you.
terms.example: You pull a drawer open. A bullock pulls a cart.
terms.art: A bullock pulling a cart, the arrow pointing forward along the rope.

terms.meaning: A turning force. It is a push on one side and a pull on the other side at the same time.
terms.example: Opening a tap or a jar lid is a twist.
terms.art: A hand turning a tap, one arrow pushing on one side and one pulling on the other.

terms.meaning: The way something is going or pointing. Up, down, left, right, forwards and backwards are all directions.
terms.example: A carrom striker flicked to the left goes left. Flicked forwards, it goes forwards.
terms.art: A carrom board with three arrows from the striker, each a different direction.

terms.meaning: A drawing that shows a force. The arrow starts on the thing being pushed or pulled. It points the way the force goes. A longer arrow means a bigger force.
terms.example: A short arrow for a gentle push on a box, and a long arrow for a hard push.
terms.art: A box with a short arrow and the same box with a long arrow.

terms.meaning: How big or strong a force is. A gentle tap is a small force. A hard shove is a big force.
terms.example: Lifting a feather needs a tiny force. Lifting a bucket of water needs a big one.
terms.art: A feather on one finger and a child straining to lift a bucket.

terms.meaning: A force that works only when two things touch.
terms.example: Your hand pushing a swing. The floor pushing up on your feet.
terms.art: A hand on a swing seat, the touching place glowing.

terms.meaning: A force that can push or pull without touching. Scientists call it a non-contact force.
terms.example: A magnet pulls a pin from across the table. The Earth pulls a falling mango down.
terms.art: A magnet pulling a pin through the air, with a dotted line between them.

terms.meaning: The pull that every object has on every other object. The Earth's gravity pulls everything towards the middle of the Earth.
terms.example: A mango falls down from the tree, never up.
terms.art: A mango falling from a tree, an arrow pointing down towards the ground.

terms.meaning: The push or pull of a magnet. Magnets pull on iron and steel. Two magnets can pull together or push apart.
terms.example: A fridge magnet holds a list on the steel door.
terms.art: Two bar magnets, one pair pulling together and one pair pushing apart.

terms.meaning: Two or more forces that cancel each other out. Balanced forces do not change how something moves.
terms.example: Two equal teams in a tug of war. The rope stays still.
terms.art: A tug of war rope with two arrows the same length pointing opposite ways.

terms.meaning: Forces that do not cancel out. Unbalanced forces change how something moves.
terms.example: One team pulls harder, so the rope starts to move that way.
terms.art: A tug of war rope with one long arrow and one short arrow.

terms.meaning: Every force comes with a partner. When you push or pull something, it pushes or pulls you back just as hard, the opposite way.
terms.example: Push a wall and the wall pushes you. A balloon pushes air out, and the air pushes the balloon forward.
terms.art: A child pushing a wall, one arrow on the wall and an equal arrow pointing back at the child.

terms.meaning: The pull along a rope, a string or a chain when it is pulled tight. A rope can only pull. It can never push.
terms.example: The rope of a well bucket is in tension when the bucket hangs from it.
terms.art: A bucket hanging from a well rope, a small arrow pointing up along the rope.

terms.meaning: The push of a floor, a table or a chair holding something up. Scientists call it the normal force.
terms.example: The table pushes up on your plate, so the plate does not fall through.
terms.art: A plate on a table with one arrow down for gravity and one arrow up from the table.

terms.meaning: The push that moves a rocket, a boat or a balloon forward. It comes from pushing something else backwards.
terms.example: A boatman pushes water back with an oar. The water pushes the boat forward.
terms.art: A rowing boat, the oar pushing water back and an arrow pushing the boat forward.

terms.meaning: The soft parts of your body that move you. A muscle can only pull, by getting shorter. It can never push.
terms.example: The muscle at the front of your upper arm pulls to bend your elbow.
terms.art: An arm bending, with the front upper-arm muscle drawn bunched up and an arrow pulling.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: Your hand, the wall and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a hand to its skin to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: An even tinier bit on the outside of every atom. Electrons carry electric charge, so electrons push other electrons away.
terms.example: When your hand presses on a wall, the electrons of your hand and the wall push each other apart.
terms.art: Two atoms side by side, their electron clouds nudging each other apart.

terms.meaning: The unit for measuring the size of a force. It is named after the scientist Isaac Newton. You will learn to measure newtons in the forcemeters unit.
terms.example: Holding up a small apple takes a force of about 1 newton.
terms.art: A hand holding a small apple, '1 newton' written beside it.

terms.meaning: Anything that has both a size and a direction, so it is drawn as an arrow. Forces are vectors. So is the wind.
terms.example: A weather map shows the wind as arrows. The arrow says which way and how strong.
terms.art: A weather map of India with wind arrows sweeping in from the sea.

explanations.definition: A force is a push or a pull on something. Forces change how things move, and they can change their shape.
explanations.description: Nothing starts moving by itself. A ball on the floor stays still until something pushes it. Once it is rolling, something has to push against it to stop it. That push or pull is a force. You cannot see a force. You can only see what it does. Some actions are a push and a pull at once. Turning a tap is a push on one side and a pull on the other. We call that a twist.
examples: Opening the fridge is a pull. Closing it is a push.
Squeezing toothpaste is a push. Picking up a school bag is a pull.
Turning a key in a lock is a twist.
explanations.art: A kitchen scene full of arrows: a hand pulling the fridge door, a thumb pushing a switch, fingers twisting a tap.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a force is.

explanations.concept: What forces do to moving things
explanations.definition: A force can start a thing moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down or change its direction.
explanations.description: Think of one cricket ball in one over. The bowler's push starts it moving. The bat's push changes its direction and speeds it up. The air and the grass slow it down. The fielder's hands stop it. Each change needs a force. If no force acts, nothing changes. A still thing stays still, and a moving thing keeps going the same way. Forces can also squash, stretch and twist things out of shape. That is a whole unit of its own, called Forces change shape.
examples: Start: you push a toy car and it begins to roll.
Stop: a goalkeeper catches the ball.
Speed up: you push a swing as it moves away from you.
Slow down: you put your feet down on a cycle.
Change direction: a carrom coin hits the edge of the board and bounces off sideways.
explanations.art: A cricket ball's journey in five small panels, each with an arrow: bowled, hit, slowing on grass, caught.
explanations.context: This card follows one cricket ball to show the five jobs a force can do to a moving thing.

explanations.definition: Every force acts in a direction. The same force in a different direction has a different result.
explanations.description: Push a carrom striker forwards and it goes forwards. Push it the same amount to the left and it goes left. The push was just as big. Only its direction changed. So to describe a force, you must say two things. How big is it? Which way does it point? Pulling a door handle towards you opens the door. Pushing the same handle away shuts it. A push on the side of a moving ball turns it. A push from behind speeds it up. A push from the front slows it down.
examples: Pushing a swing from behind speeds it up. Pushing it from the front slows it down.
A batsman can send the same ball to the left or right of the field, just by changing the angle of the bat.
Pushing down on a table does not move it. Pushing sideways can slide it.
explanations.art: A swing seen from the side twice: a hand pushing from behind with a forward arrow, then a hand pushing from the front with a backward arrow.
explanations.context: This card shows that a force is not just strong or weak. It always points one way, and the way matters.

explanations.definition: Scientists draw a force as an arrow. The arrow starts on the thing the force acts on. It points the way the force goes. Its length shows how big the force is.
explanations.description: An arrow is the perfect drawing for a force, because an arrow has a length and a direction. Here are the three rules. One: start the arrow on the thing being pushed or pulled. Two: point it the way of the push or pull. Three: draw a longer arrow for a bigger force. Then write what the force is next to it, for example 'my push' or 'gravity'. A thing can have many arrows on it at once. A book on a table has an arrow down for gravity, and an arrow up for the table's push. Anything with a size and a direction, drawn as an arrow, is called a vector. Weather maps draw the wind as vectors. Ship captains and pilots use them every day.
examples: A gentle push on a box gets a short arrow. A hard push gets an arrow twice as long.
A kite on a string has an arrow along the string, pulling towards the person holding it.
India's weather maps show the monsoon wind as arrows sweeping in from the sea.
explanations.art: A box with three arrows of different lengths pushing it, each labelled, and a small key: longer arrow, bigger force.
explanations.context: This card teaches the three rules for drawing a force as an arrow. Arrows appear all through this unit.

explanations.concept: Adding forces: when do they balance?
explanations.definition: When forces point the same way, they add up. When they point opposite ways, they work against each other. If they cancel out, they are balanced and nothing changes. If they do not, they are unbalanced and the motion changes.
explanations.description: Imagine a tug of war. On one side, three children pull. On the other side, two children pull. If every child pulls the same amount, the side with three wins. The forces are unbalanced. Now give the two children a grown-up. If both sides pull equally, the rope does not move. The forces are balanced. Balanced does not mean no forces. It means the forces cancel. A book lying on a table has two balanced forces on it. Gravity pulls it down, and the table pushes it up just as hard. You will go much further with this in Class 4, in the unit on balanced forces.
examples: Two children push a box from opposite sides equally hard. It stays put.
Two children push a heavy box from the same side. Their pushes add up and it moves more easily.
A hanging lamp is still. The cord pulls it up, and gravity pulls it down, equally.
explanations.art: Two tug of war pictures: arrows of equal length and a still rope, then one long and one short arrow and the rope sliding.
explanations.context: Remember the tug of war, where two teams pull a rope? This card shows how to add up pulls with arrows to say which way the rope will go.

explanations.concept: Every push gets a push back
explanations.definition: Forces always come in pairs. When one thing pushes or pulls another, the second thing pushes or pulls back on the first, just as hard, in the opposite direction. This is Newton's third law of motion.
explanations.description: Push against a wall and you feel it push your hands. If you are on a skateboard, you roll backwards. The wall pushed you. Isaac Newton wrote this rule down in 1687, in a book called the Principia. The two forces in a pair act on different things. Your push acts on the wall. The wall's push acts on you. This rule explains how we move at all. To walk forward, your foot pushes the ground backwards. The ground pushes you forwards. A swimmer pushes water back, and the water pushes the swimmer forward. A rocket pushes hot gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.
examples: A balloon lets out its air. It pushes the air backwards, and the air pushes the balloon forwards.
Jump off a small boat and the boat moves backwards.
A boatman on the backwaters pushes a long pole against the river bed. The river bed pushes the boat along.
explanations.art: A child on a skateboard pushing a wall, two equal arrows: one on the wall pointing at it, one on the child pointing back.
explanations.context: When you push something, does it push you? This card explains one of the most important rules in physics: forces come in pairs.

explanations.concept: Pushes and pulls from far away
explanations.definition: Some forces only work when things touch. These are contact forces. Others can push or pull across a gap. These are forces at a distance, also called non-contact forces. Gravity, magnetic forces and electric forces can act at a distance.
explanations.description: Most pushes and pulls need touching. You cannot push a swing without touching it. But a magnet can pull a pin from across the table. A balloon rubbed on your hair can pull little bits of paper up into the air. And the Earth pulls a mango down from a tree without any rope. Gravity even reaches out to the Moon, about 3,84,000 kilometres away, and holds it in its path. How a pull can cross empty space puzzled even Isaac Newton. He wrote, in 1713, that he would not make up a guess about how gravity works.
examples: A magnet under a sheet of paper drags a paper clip on top of it.
A rubbed balloon makes your hair stand up towards it.
The Moon's gravity pulls on the sea and helps make the tides.
explanations.art: Three panels: a magnet pulling a clip through paper, a balloon lifting bits of paper, and the Earth pulling the Moon with a faint dotted arrow.
explanations.context: Can you push or pull something without touching it? This card is about forces that work across a gap.

explanations.concept: Some things can only pull: ropes and muscles
explanations.definition: A rope, a string or a chain can only pull. So can a muscle. None of them can push.
explanations.description: Try to push a ball across the floor with a piece of string. The string just folds up. Ropes only work when they are pulled tight. Your muscles are the same. A muscle can only get shorter and pull on a bone. It cannot get longer by itself and push. So muscles work in pairs. To bend your arm, the muscle on the front of your upper arm pulls. To straighten it, the muscle on the back pulls instead. Your heart is a muscle too. It squeezes inwards, and the squeeze pushes blood out round your body. Inside every cell, tiny machines called motor proteins walk along thin tracks. They pull loads behind them, one tiny step at a time.
examples: Feel the front of your upper arm as you bend your elbow. It bunches up as it pulls.
Puppets on strings can only be pulled, never pushed, by the strings.
A crane lifts things with a cable. It always pulls up, never pushes down.
explanations.art: An arm in two positions, front muscle bunched and pulling when bent, back muscle bunched and pulling when straight.
explanations.context: Can a rope push? Can your muscles? This card is about things that can only pull, and how the body works around that.

explanations.concept: Plants and nature push and pull too
explanations.definition: Pushes and pulls are not only made by people and animals. Wind, water, growing plants and the Earth itself push and pull all the time.
explanations.description: A growing seedling pushes up through the soil. Tree roots push so hard as they grow that they can crack a footpath. Mushrooms sometimes push up through a tarred road. Rivers push sand and stones along, all the way to the sea. The wind pushes sailing boats and kites. Inside the Earth, huge slabs of rock slowly push against each other. Over millions of years, the push of India against Asia lifted up the Himalayas. That push has not stopped. The mountains are still rising, a few millimetres a year.
examples: A peepal tree growing out of a crack in an old wall slowly pushes the bricks apart.
The monsoon wind pushes clouds from the sea over the land.
India is still moving north and pushing into Asia, about 4 to 5 centimetres a year.
explanations.art: A peepal sapling splitting an old brick wall, with arrows showing the roots pushing outwards.
explanations.context: Only living things push and pull? This card shows that plants, water, wind and even whole continents do too.

explanations.description: Zoom in on your hand pressing a wall, far past anything a microscope can show. You reach atoms. The outside of each atom is a cloud of electrons. Electrons push other electrons away with electric force. So when you press the wall, the electrons of your hand and the wall push each other apart. That is the push you feel. It is also why you do not sink through the floor. So every contact force, deep down, is an electric force. This much scientists agree on. But does that mean you never really touch anything? Here people disagree, because it depends on what 'touch' means.
examples: The floor holding you up is electrons in the floor pushing on electrons in your feet.
A rope pulling is atoms in the rope holding on to their neighbours with electric force.

perspectives.explanation: You never truly touch anything. Your atoms always stay a tiny gap away from the wall's atoms, held apart by electric pushes.
That is just what touching is. Atoms have no hard edge, so there is no gap to measure. Touching means being close enough to push each other. By that meaning, you touch things all the time.

perspectives.who: Wolfgang Pauli, an Austrian physicist, in 1925, and physicists since
perspectives.explanation: There is a second reason solids push back. A rule of quantum physics, found by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925, stops electrons from crowding into the same state. So squeezed atoms resist being pushed together.

explanations.art: A four-step zoom: a palm on a wall, skin meeting plaster, two atoms, two electron clouds pushing apart labelled 'electric push'.
explanations.context: This card zooms right down to atoms to ask a strange question: when you press on a wall, are you really touching it?

explanations.definition: Gravity is a force pair too. The Earth pulls you down, and you pull the Earth up, just as hard.
explanations.description: This sounds impossible, but it is true. When you jump, the Earth pulls you back down. At the same moment, you pull the Earth up towards you, with exactly the same size of force. So why does the Earth not move? It does, but by far too little to ever notice, because the Earth is so enormous. The same thing happens in space. The Earth pulls the Moon, and the Moon pulls the Earth. The Sun pulls the Earth, and the Earth pulls the Sun. Everything pulls everything. So right now, as you sit reading, you are pulling the whole planet.
examples: A falling mango pulls the Earth up a tiny, tiny bit as it falls.
The Moon's pull lifts the sea into tides. The Earth's pull keeps the same side of the Moon always facing us.
explanations.art: A child mid-jump above a giant Earth, a long arrow from the Earth pulling the child down and an equal arrow from the child pulling the Earth up.
explanations.context: Gravity pulls you down to the Earth. This card is about the surprising other half of that pull.

explanations.definition: Light pushes very gently on anything it hits. Scientists call this radiation pressure.
explanations.description: Sunlight on your face pushes on you, but far too gently to feel. In space, with no air and no friction, even this tiny push adds up. That is why the tail of a comet always points away from the Sun. Sunlight and a wind of tiny bits from the Sun push the comet's dust and gas outwards. Engineers have used this push to sail through space. In 2010, Japan's space agency flew a spacecraft called IKAROS. It had a huge, thin sail, and sunlight pushed it between the planets. It was the first sail of its kind to work far out in space.
examples: A comet's tail points away from the Sun, even when the comet is moving away from the Sun.
A solar sail is thinner than a hair, and as big as a room or bigger.
explanations.art: A comet passing the Sun, its tail always pointing away from the Sun, with small arrows of sunlight pushing it.
explanations.context: Can light push things? This card is about the gentlest push there is, and how it bends comet tails and sails spacecraft.

explanations.concept: Why does a thrown ball keep going?
explanations.definition: A moving thing keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction unless a force changes it. You only need a force to change motion, not to keep it going.
explanations.description: Throw a ball. Once it leaves your hand, nothing is pushing it forward. So why does it keep going? People argued about this for about 2,000 years. Here are the main answers. Only the last one is accepted today. We know because spacecraft prove it. Voyager 1 was launched in 1977. Its engines have been off for decades, yet it is still coasting away from us, now more than 24 billion kilometres from Earth.
examples: A carrom coin keeps sliding after you flick it, until friction stops it.
In a space station, a pushed pen floats across the room in a straight line until it hits a wall.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Moving things stop by themselves unless something keeps pushing them. A thrown stone is pushed along by the air rushing in behind it.

perspectives.who: The Vaiśeṣika school of Kaṇāda, in ancient India, more than 2,000 years ago (scholars disagree on the exact date)
perspectives.explanation: They studied a flying arrow. The first movement comes from the push of the bowstring, which they called nodana. After that, the arrow keeps moving because of a moving-tendency the push gave it, called vega or saṃskāra. It slowly fades.

perspectives.who: John Philoponus in Alexandria, about 1,500 years ago, Ibn Sina in Persia, about 1,000 years ago, and Jean Buridan in France, about 700 years ago
perspectives.explanation: The air does not push the stone. The thrower puts something into the stone, a kind of inner push, and the stone uses it up as the air and ground resist it.

perspectives.who: Galileo in Italy, about 400 years ago, and Isaac Newton in England, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: Nothing gets used up. A moving thing simply keeps moving until a force, like friction or air, slows it. This is Newton's first law. It is the accepted answer today.

explanations.art: A timeline of four thinkers watching the same arrow fly from a bow, each with a speech bubble.
explanations.context: When you throw a ball, nothing pushes it after it leaves your hand. This card tells how thinkers across the world tried to explain why it keeps going.

explanations.description: We can measure forces very well. We can predict where rockets will go. But what a force really is turns out to be a deep question. Different great thinkers have answered it differently, and the question is not settled.
examples: Two magnets push apart across a gap with nothing visible between them.
The Earth pulls the Moon across 3,84,000 kilometres of nearly empty space.

perspectives.explanation: A force is whatever changes a thing's motion. He described gravity exactly, but he refused to guess what it is made of.

perspectives.who: Heinrich Hertz, a German physicist, in a book published in 1894
perspectives.explanation: Perhaps forces are not real things at all. He tried to write all of mechanics using only movement, with no forces in it.
Gravity is not a pull. Heavy things bend space and time around them, and other things follow the bends. Experiments since 1919 keep showing he was right.

Forces are carried by tiny particles passing between things. Light particles, called photons, carry the electric force. Some physicists think gravity is carried by a particle called the graviton, but nobody has ever found one.

explanations.art: Two magnets pushing apart, with four thought bubbles above them showing an arrow, a question mark, a bent sheet of space, and tiny particles flying between.
explanations.context: This card goes to the frontier. Scientists can measure every push and pull, but they still argue about what a force really is.

agreed.text: A force is a push or a pull, and it always acts in a direction.
agreed.evidence: Every push we measure has a size and a way it points. Change the direction of the same push and the result changes. Engineers rely on this to build every bridge, crane and rocket.

agreed.text: Forces change motion. A force is needed to start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn something, but not to keep it moving.
agreed.evidence: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977. Its engines have long been switched off, yet it keeps coasting away from the Sun. On Earth, things only stop because friction and air push against them.

agreed.text: Forces come in pairs that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
agreed.evidence: Hook two spring forcemeters together and pull them apart. Both always show the same number. Rockets work in empty space because of this rule.

agreed.text: Gravity, magnetic forces and electric forces can act across a gap, without touching.
agreed.evidence: A magnet pulls a clip through a sheet of paper. Spacecraft travel by the pull of planets millions of kilometres away.

agreed.text: Deep down, almost every push and pull in daily life is an electric force between atoms. Physicists know of four basic forces in all: gravity, the electromagnetic force, and two forces that act only inside atoms.
agreed.evidence: Experiments since the 1800s showed that light, electricity and magnetism are one force. Experiments in the 1900s found the two forces inside atoms.

challenging.claim: A moving thing needs a push to keep it going.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago. Most of us also feel this without noticing.
challenging.for: Push a box and stop pushing, and it stops. A cycle slows down when you stop pedalling.
challenging.against: Things only stop because friction and air push against them. Galileo saw that a ball rolls further on smoother ground. In space, with nothing to slow it, a pushed thing keeps going. Voyager 1 has coasted for nearly 50 years.
challenging.context: This card is about a very old idea of how pushing and moving are linked.

challenging.claim: In a tug of war, the rope pulls the losing team harder than the winning team.
challenging.who: A common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: The losing team gets dragged forward, so it feels as if the rope beat them.
challenging.against: A rope that is tight pulls equally hard at both ends. The winning team wins by pushing harder on the ground with their feet. The ground then pushes them back, away from the middle line.
challenging.context: In a tug of war, two teams pull on the ends of one rope. This card asks who the rope pulls harder.

challenging.claim: If you push something and it does not move, there is no force.
challenging.for: Nothing happened, so it seems nothing was there.
challenging.against: Your push is real. It is balanced by another force, for example the floor gripping the box, or the wall pushing back. A wall even bends a tiny bit when you push it, too little to see.
challenging.context: Have you ever pushed a heavy almirah and it did not budge? This card asks whether there was any force at all.

challenging.claim: Rockets cannot work in space, because there is no air there to push against.
challenging.who: A newspaper, The New York Times, in 1920, mocking the rocket scientist Robert Goddard
challenging.for: On Earth, a swimmer pushes water and a bird pushes air. It seemed a rocket must need air to push on too.
challenging.against: A rocket pushes its own hot gases out backwards, and the gases push the rocket forwards. No air is needed. In July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon, the newspaper printed a correction.
challenging.context: Robert Goddard was an American scientist who built some of the first liquid-fuel rockets. This card is about people who said his rockets could never fly in space.

challenging.claim: Gravity is not really a pull at all. Heavy things bend space and time, and other things follow the bends.
challenging.for: His idea predicted that starlight would bend round the Sun. This was seen in 1919, and in many experiments since. Satellite navigation in phones must use his idea, or it goes wrong.
challenging.against: Thinking of gravity as Newton's pull still works almost everywhere, and engineers use it to send spacecraft to other planets. Some physicists hope to describe gravity as a force carried by particles, like the other forces. Nobody has managed it yet.
challenging.context: Most of us learn that gravity is a pull. This card is about a famous idea that says it is something stranger.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton alone discovered the laws of force.
challenging.for: Newton wrote the three laws of motion together, clearly, in one book in 1687.
challenging.against: He built on Galileo, René Descartes, Christiaan Huygens and others. Robert Hooke argued with him about the idea of gravity. And for many readers it was a woman, Émilie du Châtelet, who made the book understandable. She translated it into French with her own notes. Her translation came out in 1759, ten years after she died, and is still used today.
challenging.context: Isaac Newton wrote down three famous laws about forces in 1687. This card asks who should share the credit.

big_questions.q: You can't see a force. You can only see what it does. So how do we know forces are real?
big_questions.hint: Push your palm against a friend's palm. What do you feel? Is feeling a kind of seeing?

big_questions.q: When you jump, you pull the whole Earth up towards you a tiny bit. Why don't you notice?
big_questions.hint: Think of an ant pushing an elephant. Who moves more?

big_questions.q: If you push a wall, the wall pushes back. Is the wall doing it on purpose?
big_questions.hint: Does a thing need to be alive, or to want something, to push?

big_questions.q: A rope can only pull, and a muscle can only pull. How does your body push a door, if all its muscles only pull?
big_questions.hint: Watch your arm straighten. Which muscle is pulling now, and where does it pull the bone?

big_questions.q: In a tug of war, the rope pulls both teams equally. So what decides who wins?
big_questions.hint: Look down, not at the rope. Where are the winners' feet?

big_questions.q: The Sun pulls the Earth, the Earth pulls you, and you pull everything around you. Is anything in the universe truly alone?
big_questions.hint: Can you think of anything that nothing pulls on at all?

big_questions.q: Every push gets a push back. When you are unkind to someone, does something push back? Is that the same kind of rule, or just a nice story?
big_questions.hint: A science rule can be tested. How would you test a rule about people?

big_questions.q: When two people pull the same way, their pulls add up. When they pull against each other, they cancel out. What does your family pull together on?
big_questions.hint: Think of moving a heavy almirah, or planning a festival.

big_questions.q: Newton got the fame, but Émilie du Châtelet made his book readable for a whole country. Who should get the credit for an idea: the person who finds it, or the people who help everyone understand it?
big_questions.hint: Think of a teacher who explained something so you finally understood.

big_questions.q: Scientists can measure every force, but still argue about what a force really is. Can you use something well without knowing what it is?
big_questions.hint: Do you know what electricity really is? You still switch on the fan.

big_questions.q: Sunlight pushes on you right now, too gently to feel. What other tiny pushes might be all around us, that we never notice?
big_questions.hint: Think of the air pressing on you, a breeze, or the floor holding you up.

story.title: The Rope That Could Only Pull
story.note: Onam's tug of war, called vadamvali, is real, and so are the coir rope makers of Alappuzha in Kerala. The rope, Anjali, her mother and the two teams are made up. The physics is true: a tight rope pulls equally at both ends, and the team that pushes the ground harder wins.
text: I was born on a beach in Alappuzha, in Kerala, out of coconut husks. Women soaked the husks in the backwaters for months. They beat them into soft brown hair, and spun the hair into yarn on wheels that hummed all day. Then they twisted the yarn into strands, and the strands into me. I am thirty metres long and as thick as a child's wrist. Every twist in me was made by a woman's hands.

I learned the first fact about myself very early. I cannot push. Hold one end of me and push it towards the other end, and I only fold into a heap, like a sleepy snake. Ropes can only pull. When I am pulled tight, every fibre in me holds on to the next fibre, all the way along. That holding on is my whole life.

For eleven years I have lived in the storeroom of a village school beside the river. I come out once a year, at Onam, the harvest festival, for the vadamvali. That is the tug of war. And for eleven years, the boatmen have won.

The boatmen row the long snake boats in the races. Their arms are like young coconut trunks. Every year they take one end of me, and another team takes the other end. Every year, after a lot of shouting, I slide across the chalk line towards the boatmen. People say the boatmen pull harder.

Here is a secret that only a rope knows. While I am stretched tight between two teams, I am pulled exactly as hard at one end as at the other. I feel it in every twist. If the boatmen pull me with the strength of ten men, the other team is pulling me with the strength of ten men too. Nobody believes this, because nobody asks the rope.

This year, the other team was the coir spinners. Some of them were daughters and granddaughters of the women who made me. Their team was one short, so they let a girl of nine join them. Her name was Anjali. She was small, with a long plait and a scab on one knee, and she held me as if I might bite.

The first round went the way it always did. The spinners gripped me and pulled with their arms, standing tall, as if lifting a bucket from a well. The boatmen crouched low, dug their heels into the wet earth and walked backwards, step by step. I slid. The crowd laughed kindly. One round to the boatmen.

Between rounds, the spinners sat on the grass to rest their hands. Anjali did not rest. She sat beside me and laid her palm on me. She was quiet for a long time. She was not looking at me. She was looking at the boatmen's feet.
'Amma,' she said at last, 'when the boatmen pulled harder, did the rope pull us harder?'
'Of course,' said her mother, rubbing her palms.
'Then it pulled them harder too,' said Anjali. 'It's one rope. It can't pull one end more than the other.'
Her mother laughed. 'Then how do they always win?'

Anjali did not answer. She stood up and pressed one bare foot hard into the ground, as if starting a race. She leaned back against nothing. 'The rope isn't what moves them,' she said slowly. 'The ground is. They push the ground towards the middle with their heels. And the ground pushes them back, the other way. We didn't push the ground at all. We just held on.'

She picked up a stick and drew in the mud. First she drew a long arrow pointing away from the chalk line. 'That's where we want to go.' Then, under it, she drew a short arrow pointing the other way. 'That's where our feet must push.' The spinners looked at the arrows. They looked at each other. Then one of the old women, who had spun yarn for forty years, began to laugh. It was the laugh of somebody who has just seen a thing that was always in front of her.

In the second round, the spinners did not stand tall. They crouched low, like the boatmen. They dug their heels into the mud. And they moved together, the way their mothers had always twisted yarn together, to a song. One, two, push. One, two, push.

I felt it. I was not pulled any harder at their end. I am never pulled harder at one end. But now the spinners were moving away from the line, one push at a time. The ground was pushing them back, and they were bringing me with them. The boatmen, who had stood up straight to laugh, sat down very suddenly in the mud.

The spinners won the second round. In the third round, the boatmen crouched again and pushed with all their strength. For a long time, nobody moved at all. I hung over the chalk line, stretched so tight that I sang a little. Two teams, pulling equally, pushing the ground equally. Then a boatman's heel slipped on the wet grass. The spinners did not slip. They had found the dry patch, because Anjali had been looking at the ground all day.

Afterwards, the boatmen's captain came to look at the arrows in the mud. He was a big man with a grey moustache. He crouched beside Anjali, and she explained the arrows to him. He nodded slowly and scratched his head.

Tonight I am back in the storeroom, coiled in the dark, smelling of mud and coconut. For eleven years, everybody watched me. Everybody thought the answer was in the rope. A girl of nine was the first one to look at the ground. Somewhere in me there is a twist her grandmother made. I like to think it held on a little tighter today.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the rope is pulled equally at both ends, so 'pulling harder on the rope' cannot be what wins. Every pull needs a push. Each team's feet push the ground towards the middle, and the ground pushes the team back the other way. Whichever team gets the bigger push from the ground wins. Anjali solves it by drawing force arrows: the way she wants to go, and the opposite way her feet must push. The story also asks who notices things, and whose hands made what everyone else uses.
ask: The rope says it is always pulled equally hard at both ends. If that is true, how can one team win?
Anjali drew two arrows in the mud. Which way did each one point, and why?
Why do you think nobody noticed the answer for eleven years?
The old spinner laughed when she understood. Have you ever laughed when you suddenly understood something?
Who made the rope? Why do you think the rope tells us that at the very beginning?

games.title: Arrow Wars: the tug of war card game
games.players: 2 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 30 arrow cards to cut out
items: Arrow length 4 (a very strong pull), 4 cards
SWAP: swap one of your arrows with your opponent's
PUSH THE GROUND: double your shortest arrow this round
SLIP: your opponent's longest arrow is cancelled
FRIEND JOINS: add one more card from the pile

printables.title: A tug of war board
items: A rope drawn across the middle, with a chalk line in the centre
5 squares on each side of the line, numbered 1 to 5
A marker token for the middle of the rope

printables.title: Arrow sum sheet
items: Which way the rope moves, and how many squares

rules: Put the rope marker on the chalk line. Shuffle the arrow cards and deal 5 to each player.
Each round, both players secretly choose 2 arrow cards and lay them face down on their side of the rope.
Turn the cards over. Each player adds up the lengths of their arrows.
Take the smaller total from the bigger total. Move the rope marker that many squares towards the player with the bigger total.
If the totals are the same, the forces are balanced. The marker does not move.
Special cards change the round as they say. Draw back up to 5 cards after each round.
The first player to pull the marker onto their square 5 wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board on the floor or a table. 2. Put the marker on the chalk line. 3. Shuffle the arrow cards and deal 5 to each player.
flow.say: Each arrow card is a pull on the rope. A longer arrow is a bigger pull. Each round, you both pull with two cards. Let's see which way the rope goes.
flow.kid: Put the marker on the middle line. Deal 5 cards each. Each arrow is a pull. A longer arrow pulls harder.
flow.context: This is the first step of Arrow Wars, a card game about tug of war. You add up force arrows to find which way the rope moves.

flow.do: Play one practice round with the cards face up. Pick a 3 and a 1 for one side, and a 2 and a 2 for the other.
flow.say: One side has a 3 and a 1. That makes 4. The other side has a 2 and a 2. That also makes 4. Which way does the rope go?
flow.kid: Practice round. One side has arrows 3 and 1. The other has 2 and 2. Which way does the rope go?

good: Both sides pull 4.
The pulls are balanced. They cancel out.

check.q: One side pulls with arrows of 3 and 1. The other side pulls with 2 and 2. What happens?
options: The rope moves towards the 3 and 1
The rope stays still, because 4 and 4 are balanced
The rope moves towards the 2 and 2
check.why: In the game, both sides total 4, so the pulls balance and the marker stays on the line. Moving it towards one side usually means only one card was counted, not the total.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds until someone wins. 2. After each round, both players say their total out loud. 3. Then say the difference, and move the marker.
flow.say: Say your total. Now take away the smaller total from the bigger one. That's how far the rope moves.
flow.kid: Turn your cards over. Add up your arrows. Take away the smaller total. Move the marker that many squares.
flow.parent: The game practises two big ideas. Pulls the same way add up. Pulls opposite ways take away from each other. Notice the PUSH THE GROUND card. It is a reminder that tug of war is won by pushing the ground with your feet. If your child says 'it's balanced' for equal totals, praise that word.

flow.do: After a few rounds, ask your child to draw one round as arrows on the rope.
flow.say: Draw the last round on paper. Draw each team's total as one arrow. Make the arrow as many centimetres long as the total.
flow.kid: Draw the last round. Draw one arrow for each team. Make each arrow as long as its total, in centimetres.
flow.think: Two small pulls the same way can beat one big pull. Where else do lots of small efforts beat one big one?

flow.do: Count who won. Then ask the big question.
flow.say: In a real tug of war, the rope pulls both teams equally hard. So what really decides who wins?
flow.kid: Who won? Now a puzzle. A real rope pulls both teams equally. So what really decides the winner?
flow.parent: A good answer: the team that pushes harder on the ground with their feet. The ground pushes them back, away from the middle. If your child is unsure, leave it as a puzzle. The story and the Push the Wall experiment come back to it.

games.context: This is a card game about tug of war. Each card is an arrow that stands for a pull. Players add up their arrows to find which way the rope will move.

setup.caption: 2. Each player picks two arrow cards, face down.

games.title: Push, Pull or Both? Force charades

printables.title: 30 action cards to cut out
items: BONUS: a magnet picking up pins
BONUS: a mango falling from a tree
BONUS: a balloon rubbed on hair, pulling up bits of paper
BONUS: a seedling pushing up through soil
BONUS: a bird flapping its wings
BONUS: the Moon pulling the sea
BONUS: the wind pushing a sailing boat
BONUS: a comet's tail pushed by sunlight

printables.title: Three answer mats
items: BOTH: a push and a pull together

printables.title: 20 arrow tokens (paper arrows to cut out)

rules: Shuffle the action cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take a card and act it out without words.
The others guess the action. The first right guess wins an arrow token.
Then everyone points to the right mat: PUSH, PULL or BOTH. Then everyone points in the direction of the force with one arm.
BONUS cards are forces you cannot act with your hands. Act them out with your whole body. For each bonus card, also say: is it a touching force or a force from far away?
When the cards run out, the player with the most arrow tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats: PUSH, PULL and BOTH. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
flow.say: Every action on these cards needs a force. You'll act one out with no words. Then we decide together. Is it a push, a pull, or both?
flow.kid: Lay out the mats. Shuffle the cards. Act out each card with no words. Then decide: push, pull or both?
flow.context: This is the first step of Force charades. Players act out everyday actions and decide whether each one is a push, a pull or both.

flow.do: 1. Take turns acting out cards. 2. After each guess, everyone points to a mat. 3. Then everyone points one arm the way the force goes.
flow.say: Which mat? Now point your arm the way the force goes. Is everyone pointing the same way?
flow.kid: Act out your card. Others guess. Point to the right mat. Then point your arm the way the force goes.

ask.q: Turning a tap. Is it a push or a pull?
good: Both. One side of my hand pushes, and the other side pulls.
It's a twist, so both.

ask.q: Drawing water from a well. Which way does the force on the bucket point?
good: Up, along the rope.
Towards my hands.

flow.parent: Some cards have more than one good answer. Brushing teeth is a push and a pull, back and forth. Rolling a chapati is mostly a push. Rowing is a pull on the oar, which pushes the water back. Reward good reasons, not only the expected answer.

flow.do: When a BONUS card comes up, act it out with your whole body. Then decide: touching force, or force from far away?
flow.say: This one has no hands in it. Is it a touching force, or does it work from far away?
flow.kid: A BONUS card! Act it out with your whole body. Then say: does this force touch, or work from far away?

check.q: A magnet picks up pins without touching most of them. What kind of force is that?
check.why: A magnet pulls across a gap, so it is a force from far away. Picking 'touching force' usually comes from seeing the pins stuck to the magnet at the end. The pull started before they touched.

flow.parent: Forces from far away on the cards: the magnet, the falling mango, the rubbed balloon, the Moon pulling the sea. The sunlight pushing a comet's tail touches it, in a way, but it comes from 150 million kilometres away. That one is a good argument to have.

flow.do: Count tokens to find the winner. Then look at the three piles of cards.
flow.say: Look at the piles. Were there more pushes, more pulls, or more of both?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Look at the piles. More pushes or more pulls?
flow.think: Your muscles can only pull. So how did you act out all those pushes?

games.context: This is an acting game. Players mime everyday actions, then decide whether each is a push, a pull or both, and which way it points.

items.p: What is a force?
opts: Only something that makes things go fast
items.why: A force is any push or pull. Picking 'only living things' is a common idea. But magnets, wind and the Earth push and pull too.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a push or a pull?
items: lifting a bucket from a well
flying a kite on its string
items.why: A push moves something away from you or presses on it. A pull moves something towards you or drags it along.

items.p: Turning a tap is…
opts: A twist: a push on one side and a pull on the other
items.why: Your fingers push on one side of the tap and pull on the other, so it turns. Picking only a push or only a pull is close, but misses the other side of the hand.

items.p: Match each moment to what the force did.
pairs: You push a toy car on the floor
A batsman hits the ball to the side
You push a swing from behind as it swings away
items.why: Forces start, stop, speed up, slow down and turn moving things.

items.p: A force always acts in a ____. That is why we draw it as an arrow.
items.why: Every force points some way. An arrow shows which way.

items.p: You draw a gentle push on a box and a hard push on the same box. Which should have the longer arrow?
items.why: A longer arrow means a bigger force. Picking 'both the same' often means the arrow is seen as just a direction. It shows the size too.

items.p: Where should a force arrow start?
opts: On the thing being pushed or pulled
At the edge of the page
items.why: The arrow starts on the thing the force acts on, and points the way the force goes.

items.p: If something is not moving, there are no forces on it.
items.why: False. A book on a table has gravity pulling it down and the table pushing it up. The two forces balance, so it stays still.

items.p: In a gentle tug of war, both sides pull equally hard. What happens to the rope?
opts: It stays still, because the pulls are balanced
items.why: Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out. They are balanced. Picking left or right means one side was imagined as stronger.

items.p: Look at the chart. In a tug of war, the left team pulls with 5 and the right team pulls with 3. Which way does the rope move?
items.why: 5 is bigger than 3, so the forces are unbalanced. The rope moves towards the left team. Picking 'right' usually means the shorter bar was read as the winner.
items.context: In a tug of war, two teams pull a rope in opposite directions. The bigger total pull wins.

chart.title: The pulls in the tug of war

items.p: You sit on a towel and push a wall with your feet. You slide away from the wall. What pushed you?
items.why: When you push the wall, the wall pushes you back, just as hard. Picking 'nothing' is very common. But you cannot start moving without a force.

items.p: A balloon lets its air rush out backwards. Which way does the balloon go?
items.why: The balloon pushes the air backwards, so the air pushes the balloon forwards. Picking 'backwards' means the balloon was pictured being carried along with the air.

items.p: Sort these forces. Do they need touching, or can they work from far away?
items: the Earth pulling a falling mango
a rubbed balloon lifting bits of paper
pulling a cart with a rope
items.why: Gravity, magnetic pulls and electric pulls can work across a gap. Most other pushes and pulls need touching.

items.p: A rope can push a ball across the floor.
items.why: False. A rope only works when it is pulled tight. Push it and it just folds up.

items.p: A book lies still on a table. Draw the forces on it with arrows.
items.why: Gravity pulls the book down. The table pushes it up just as hard. There is no push or friction, because nobody is pushing it sideways.

items.p: Name one push and one pull you used today. Say which way each one pointed.
items.a: Any one push and one pull, each with a direction. For example: I pushed the bathroom door away from me. I pulled my socks up.
items.why: Any correct push and pull, each with a direction, is right.

items.p: Draw a child pushing a box to the right. Draw an arrow for the push. Make it start on the box.
items.a: An arrow starting on the box and pointing right.
items.why: The arrow starts on the thing being pushed and points the way of the push.
items.art: An empty box on the floor, with space around it.

items.p: Two children push a heavy box from the same side. One pushes with 4 units and one with 3 units. What is the total push?
items.why: Pushes in the same direction add up. 4 + 3 = 7. Picking 1 means the pushes were taken away, which only happens when they point opposite ways.

items.p: Now the two children push from opposite sides. One pushes the box towards the right with 4 units. The other pushes it towards the left with 3 units. What happens?
opts: The box moves right with a push of 7 units
The box moves right with a push of 1 unit
The box moves left with a push of 1 unit
items.why: Opposite pushes work against each other. 4 take away 3 is 1. The bigger push points right, so the box is pushed right with 1 unit. Picking 7 means the pushes were added, which only happens when they point the same way.

items.p: When forces cancel out and nothing changes, we say the forces are ____.
items.why: Balanced forces cancel each other out, so the motion does not change.

items.p: A carrom striker is flicked with the same strength, once forwards and once to the left. What is different?
opts: Only the size of the push
Only the direction of the push
items.why: The strength was the same, so the size was the same. Only the direction changed, so the striker went a different way.

items.p: You blow on a ping-pong ball from the bottom of a tray, and a friend blows from the left side, at the same time. Which way does the ball go?
opts: Slantwise, towards the top right corner
items.why: Your blow pushes it up the tray. Your friend's blow pushes it to the right. The two pushes add up into a slanting push, towards the top right. Picking one straight direction means only one push was counted.

items.p: How does walking forward work?
opts: Your feet push the ground backwards, and the ground pushes you forwards
You don't need any force to walk
items.why: This is a force pair. You push the ground back, and the ground pushes you forward. Picking gravity is a common mix-up. Gravity pulls you down, not forward.

items.p: A boatman on the Kerala backwaters pushes a long pole against the river bed. Which way does the boat move?
opts: Opposite to the way he pushes the pole
items.why: He pushes the river bed one way, and the river bed pushes the pole, and the boat, the other way.
items.context: Some flat boats in Kerala are moved by a boatman pushing a long bamboo pole against the bottom of the shallow water.

items.p: In a tug of war, the rope is tight and still. The left end of the rope is pulled with a force of 300. What is the pull on the right end?
items.why: A tight, still rope is pulled equally at both ends. So the right end is also pulled with 300. Picking 600 means the two ends were added. They are the same pull, not two pulls on top of each other.
items.context: Imagine a tug of war rope that is pulled tight and is not moving.

items.p: So what decides who wins a tug of war?
opts: Which team pulls the rope harder
Which team pushes the ground harder with their feet
items.why: The rope pulls both teams equally. The winning team pushes the ground harder towards the middle. The ground pushes them back, away from the middle. Picking 'pulls the rope harder' is what nearly everyone thinks at first.

items.p: Your muscles can push as well as pull.
items.why: False. Muscles can only pull, by getting shorter. That is why they work in pairs, one to bend a joint and one to straighten it.

items.p: Which pair of arrows shows a book lying still on a table?
opts: A long arrow down and a short arrow up
Two arrows the same length, one down and one up
items.why: The table pushes up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down. So the arrows are the same length. Picking 'only down' means the table's push was forgotten.

items.p: A child sits still on a swing. Draw the forces on the child.
items.obj: a child sitting still on a swing
items.why: Gravity pulls the child down. The seat pushes up just as hard. Nobody is pushing, so there is no push arrow.

items.p: A box is being pulled to the left with a rope across a floor. Show the forces with arrows.
items.obj: a box pulled left by a rope
items.why: The rope pulls left. Friction works against the sliding, so it points right. Gravity pulls down, and the floor pushes up.

items.p: Match each thing to the force that moves it.
pairs: the air it pushes out pushes it back
A paper clip jumping to a magnet
the magnet pulls it from a distance
items.why: Every movement needs a push or a pull. Some touch, and some work from far away.

items.p: Tipu Sultan's army used iron rockets more than 200 years ago. Explain how a rocket is pushed forwards. Use the words push and backwards.
items.a: The rocket pushes hot gas out backwards. The gas pushes the rocket forwards, just as hard.
items.why: Every push has a push back. The rocket's push on the gas is paired with the gas's push on the rocket.
items.context: Tipu Sultan ruled Mysore, in south India, in the 1780s and 1790s. His army used rockets with iron cases against the British East India Company.

items.p: Why is it harder to stop a swing by pushing it from behind? Use the word direction.
items.a: Pushing from behind is the same direction the swing is going, so it speeds it up. To stop it, you must push in the opposite direction, against the way it moves.
items.why: The direction of a force decides what it does to a moving thing.

items.p: Draw a kite flying, with its string held by a child. Draw an arrow for the pull of the string on the kite.
items.a: An arrow starting on the kite, pointing along the string towards the child.
items.why: A string can only pull. It pulls the kite towards the person holding it, along the string.
items.art: A kite in the sky with its string going down to a child.

items.p: When you jump, the Earth pulls you down. What does your pull do to the Earth?
opts: It pulls the Earth up towards you, just as hard, but the Earth is so huge it barely moves
It makes the Earth spin faster
items.why: Gravity is a force pair. You pull the Earth up as hard as it pulls you down. The Earth is enormous, so it moves far too little to notice. Picking 'nothing' is what nearly everyone guesses.

items.p: Deep down, what is happening when your hand presses on a wall?
opts: Electrons in your hand and the wall push each other apart
Tiny hooks catch on each other
items.why: Contact pushes come from electric forces between atoms. Picking gravity mixes up two forces. Gravity only pulls, and it is far too weak to push your hand back.

items.p: Why does a comet's tail always point away from the Sun?
opts: Sunlight and a wind of tiny bits from the Sun push the dust and gas outwards
The comet is always moving away from the Sun
The Sun's gravity pulls the tail backwards
items.why: Light really pushes. In space, the gentle push of sunlight and the solar wind blows the tail outwards. Picking 'moving away' is a sensible guess, but the tail points away from the Sun even when the comet moves towards it.
items.context: A comet is a ball of ice and dust from the far edge of the solar system. When it comes near the Sun, it grows a long glowing tail.

items.p: A spacecraft coasting in empty space needs its engine on all the time to keep moving.
items.why: False. With nothing to slow it, it keeps going. Voyager 1 has coasted since 1977 with its main engines off. You only need a force to change motion.

items.p: Match each thinker to their idea about a thrown arrow or stone.
pairs: the air pushes it along from behind
Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika school, in ancient India
the push gives it vega, a moving-tendency, that slowly fades
it keeps going by itself until a force slows it
items.why: Thinkers in many places tried to explain why thrown things keep moving. Newton's answer, building on Galileo, is the one we use today.
items.context: When you throw a stone, nothing pushes it after it leaves your hand. Thinkers across the world have tried to explain why it keeps going.

items.p: In 1920 a newspaper said rockets could never work in space. Why were they wrong?
opts: A rocket pushes its own gas out backwards, so it needs no air to push on
Rockets are pulled by the Moon
items.why: The rocket and its gas push on each other. No outside air is needed. Picking 'there is air in space' is a common guess, but space is almost empty.
items.context: Robert Goddard was an American scientist who built early rockets. In 1920, The New York Times mocked his idea that rockets could work in space.

items.p: Einstein said gravity is not really a pull. What did he say it is?
opts: Heavy things bend space and time, and other things follow the bends
items.why: Einstein's idea, from 1915, has passed many tests, starting with starlight bending round the Sun in 1919. Newton's pull is still a very good way to calculate most things.

items.p: Physicists have found a particle that carries gravity, called the graviton.
items.why: False. Some physicists think gravitons exist, but nobody has ever found one. It is one of the big open questions.

items.p: Who translated Newton's great book on forces into French, with her own notes, so many more people could read it?
items.why: Émilie du Châtelet's translation was published in 1759, ten years after she died, and is still used. Picking Marie Curie is a common guess because she is the most famous woman scientist, but she lived over 100 years later.

items.p: Inside each of your cells, tiny machines called motor proteins carry loads along thin tracks. What do they do to their loads?
opts: They pull them along, one tiny step at a time
items.why: Motor proteins walk along tracks and pull their loads behind them. Even inside a cell, moving things needs pushes and pulls.

items.p: India is slowly pushing north into Asia. What has that push made over millions of years?
items.why: The push of India into Asia folded the rocks up into the Himalayas, and they are still rising a little each year. Picking the desert or the sea mixes up pushing rock with wind and water.

items.p: A ping-pong ball is blown from the left and from below at the same time, equally hard. Which two pushes act on it?
items.obj: a ball blown from the left and from below
items.why: A blow from the left pushes the ball right. A blow from below pushes it up. Together the ball goes slantwise, up and to the right.

items.p: Your muscles can only pull. So how can you push a door open? Explain.
items.a: My muscles pull on my bones. The bones swing like levers, and my hand at the end pushes the door. So a pull inside my body becomes a push outside it.
items.why: A good answer says that muscles pull on bones, and the bones then press on the door.

items.p: In a tug of war, the rope pulls both teams equally hard. Explain how one team can still win. Draw arrows if it helps.
items.a: The winning team pushes the ground harder with their feet, towards the middle. The ground pushes them back, away from the middle, harder than it pushes the other team. So the winners move back and drag the rope.
items.why: This is the puzzle from the unit's story. The key is the push between the feet and the ground.
items.context: In this unit's story, a rope that has been used in a tug of war for eleven years says it is always pulled equally hard at both ends.

items.p: Some books say you never really touch anything, because your atoms always stay a tiny gap apart. Do you agree? Give a reason.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer with a reason. For example: I don't agree, because touching just means being close enough to push. My hand and the wall push on each other, so they touch.
items.why: There is no single right answer. It depends on what 'touch' means. What counts is a clear reason.

items.p: Everything pulls everything with gravity. Write two sentences about what this means to you.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: I am pulling on the Moon and the Sun right now, and they are pulling on me. Nothing in the universe is completely alone.
items.why: This is a big question. Any honest answer with a reason is good.

items.p: Draw yourself standing on the Earth. Draw an arrow for the Earth pulling you, and an arrow for you pulling the Earth. How long should each arrow be?
items.a: One arrow on the child pointing down towards the Earth, and one equal arrow on the Earth pointing up towards the child.
items.why: The two pulls are a force pair, so they are the same size and point opposite ways. Each acts on a different thing.
items.art: A child standing on a small round Earth, with space for two arrows.

experiments.title: Push the Wall: does the wall push back?
experiments.question: When you push a wall, does the wall push you? Does a harder push make you go further?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You sit on a towel on a smooth floor, with your feet against the wall. You push the wall with your feet. Will you move? Which way? Will a hard push send you further than a gentle push?
experiments.fair_test: Change only how hard you push: gentle, medium and hard. Keep the same towel, the same floor and the same starting place against the wall. Try each push 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: an old towel or a flattened cardboard box to sit on
a smooth floor next to a clear wall
a measuring tape
a piece of chalk or tape to mark where you stop

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays close. Clear the floor of furniture and anything sharp. Push with your feet, not your head. Never stand on a skateboard for this.

schedule.what: Push the wall gently, medium and hard, 3 times each. Measure how far you slide.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw yourself pushing the wall, with one arrow for your push on the wall and one arrow for the wall's push on you.

setup.art: A child sitting on a folded towel on a tiled floor, knees bent, both feet flat against a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Sit on the towel. Put your feet flat on the wall.

setup.art: The same child pushing with straight legs, sliding away from the wall on the towel, a grown-up kneeling beside.
setup.caption: 2. Push the wall with your feet. Slide away.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a measuring tape from the wall to the edge of the towel, a chalk mark on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Mark where you stopped. Measure from the wall.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space on a smooth floor next to a wall. 2. Fold the towel and put it against the wall. 3. Your child sits on it, knees bent, feet flat on the wall.
flow.say: You're going to push the wall with your feet. The wall is very heavy and fixed to the house. Do you think you'll move? Which way?
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up. Sit on a towel by the wall. Put your feet flat on the wall. Will you move when you push?

ask.q: What do you think will happen when you push?
good: I'll slide away from the wall.
The wall won't move, but I will.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Push the Wall experiment. You find out whether a wall pushes you back when you push it.

flow.do: 1. Your child pushes the wall gently with both feet. 2. Mark where the back of the towel stops with chalk. 3. Measure from the wall to the mark. 4. Do it 3 times each for a gentle, a medium and a hard push.
flow.say: Push gently. Now let's measure how far you slid. Now a medium push. Now your hardest push.
flow.kid: Push gently and mark where you stop. Measure it. Then push medium, then hard. Do each push 3 times.
flow.parent: Your child pushed the wall, but they moved. Something must have pushed them. The only thing touching their feet was the wall. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one.

flow.do: Talk about what pushed your child.
flow.say: You pushed the wall towards the wall. But you moved the other way. What pushed you?
flow.kid: You pushed the wall. But you moved away from it. What pushed you?

check.q: You push a wall with your feet and slide away from it. What pushed you?
options: Nothing pushed you. You just moved
check.why: The only thing touching your feet was the wall, so the wall pushed you. Picking 'nothing' means the wall's push back was not noticed. Nothing starts moving without a force.

flow.parent: This is a force pair. Your child pushed the wall, and the wall pushed back on your child, just as hard, the opposite way. The wall does not move because it is fixed to the whole house and the Earth.

flow.do: Help your child draw two arrows of the same length. One goes on the wall, pointing into the wall. The other goes on your child, pointing away from the wall.
flow.say: Draw your push on the wall as an arrow. Now draw the wall's push on you. Should the arrows be the same length?
flow.kid: Draw an arrow for your push on the wall. Draw an arrow for the wall's push on you. Make them the same length.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the child rolled after pushing the wall
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.think: A harder push on the wall sent you further. So did the wall push you harder too?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: when I push the wall, the wall pushes me back. What I saw: my gentle push slid me about 40 cm, but my hard push slid me about 190 cm. Why: the harder I push the wall, the harder the wall pushes me.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you sit on a towel on a smooth floor and push a wall with your feet. You find out whether the wall pushes you back.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: The Balloon Rocket
experiments.question: Which way does a balloon move when it lets its air out? Does more air send it further?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the air rushes out of the balloon's neck, will the balloon go the same way as the air, or the opposite way? Will a balloon with 6 breaths go further than one with 2 breaths?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of breaths: 2, then 4, then 6. Use the same balloon, the same string and the same start. Try each one 2 or 3 times.

materials.item: a long balloon (round ones work too)
a smooth string about 5 metres long
a drinking straw
sticky tape
two chairs
a measuring tape

experiments.safety: Do not let small children put balloons in their mouths to chew. Throw away burst balloon pieces at once. A grown-up blows up balloons if the child finds it hard.

schedule.what: Build the balloon rocket. Test 2, 4 and 6 breaths. Measure how far it goes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the balloon with two arrows: one for the air pushed out backwards, and one for the push on the balloon.

setup.art: A long string threaded through a drinking straw and tied tightly between two chairs across a room.
setup.caption: 1. Thread the string through a straw. Tie it between two chairs.

setup.art: A blown-up long balloon held shut at the neck, being taped under the straw.
setup.caption: 2. Blow up the balloon. Hold the neck shut. Tape it under the straw.

setup.art: The balloon whooshing along the string, air rushing out of the neck behind it, a measuring tape on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. Measure how far it goes along the string.

flow.do: 1. Thread the string through the straw. 2. Tie each end of the string to a chair. 3. Pull the chairs apart until the string is tight.
flow.say: This string is the rocket's track. The straw will slide along it, carrying our balloon rocket.
flow.kid: Thread the string through the straw. Tie each end to a chair. Pull the chairs apart so the string is tight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Balloon Rocket experiment. You build a track for a balloon to fly along.

flow.do: 1. Blow 2 breaths into the balloon. 2. Pinch the neck shut. Do not tie it. 3. Tape the balloon under the straw, with its neck pointing towards one chair. 4. Slide it to that chair.
flow.say: Two breaths only. Hold the neck shut. Which way will the air rush out? Which way will the balloon go?
flow.kid: Blow 2 breaths into the balloon. Pinch the neck. Tape it under the straw. Which way will it go?

ask.q: Which way will the balloon go when you let go?
good: The opposite way to the air.
Away from the neck.

flow.do: 1. Let go. 2. Measure from the start to where the straw stopped. 3. Write it down. 4. Repeat with 4 breaths and 6 breaths.
flow.say: Let go! How far did it go? Now let's try 4 breaths, then 6.
flow.kid: Let go! Measure how far it went and write it down. Then try 4 breaths. Then try 6.

check.q: The air rushes out of the balloon's neck backwards. Which way does the balloon go?
options: Forwards, the opposite way to the air
check.why: The balloon pushes air backwards, and the air pushes the balloon forwards. Picking 'backwards' means the balloon was pictured being carried along with its air.

flow.parent: The balloon squeezes the air and pushes it out backwards. The air pushes the balloon forwards just as hard. That forward push is called thrust. Real rockets work the same way, with hot gas instead of air. They do not need air outside to push against.

flow.do: Compare the three distances.
flow.say: Which went furthest? Why do you think more air made it go further?
flow.kid: Which balloon went furthest? Why do you think so?

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the balloon rocket went
chart.x: Breaths of air in the balloon
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.think: Tipu Sultan's army in Mysore used iron rockets in battles more than 200 years ago. They also worked by pushing gas backwards. What do you think pushed them?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the balloon goes the opposite way to the air. What I saw: the air rushed out backwards and the balloon zoomed forwards. With 6 breaths it went much further than with 2. Why: the balloon pushes the air back, and the air pushes the balloon forward. More air means it pushes for longer.

experiments.context: In this experiment, a balloon is taped under a straw that slides along a string. When the balloon lets its air out, you see which way it goes, and how far.
